title: Storage Engines: B-Trees vs LSM
subtitle: Watch the same write travel through a B-tree and an LSM tree, and see where each one pays its cost.
learn: How a B-tree updates a page in place, and why a tiny change rewrites a whole page
How an LSM tree turns random writes into sequential ones using a memtable, SSTables, and compaction
What write amplification and read amplification mean, with realistic numbers
Why both designs need a write-ahead log (WAL) to survive crashes
How to pick an engine from the workload: read-heavy vs write-heavy

steps.title: One write, two philosophies
steps.body: Your app saves a 100-byte row. Disks, both spinning and SSD, like big sequential writes and dislike many small scattered ones. A storage engine must keep data sorted so reads are fast, yet absorb writes cheaply. The two dominant answers are the B-tree (update data in place) and the LSM tree (never update in place; merge later).
steps.idea: A storage engine balances three costs: write cost, read cost, and space.
steps.caption: Same row, two possible destinations.

steps.title: B-tree: edit the page in place
steps.body: A B-tree stores sorted rows in fixed-size pages (8 KiB in Postgres, 16 KiB in InnoDB). To change one row, the engine finds its leaf page, edits it, and eventually writes the whole page back, even for a 100-byte change. With 16 KiB InnoDB pages that is up to roughly 160x page-level write amplification (about 80x for Postgres 8 KiB pages), though several changes to one page often share a flush. Write amplification means bytes physically written divided by bytes the app asked to write. With the upper tree levels cached in RAM, a lookup usually costs about 1 disk read. Pages sit at scattered disk locations, so these are random writes.
steps.idea: B-trees make reads cheap and predictable but pay for random, page-sized writes.
steps.caption: Whole page rewritten for one small row.

steps.title: Write-ahead log first
steps.body: Edited pages live in RAM for a while, so a crash could lose them (torn pages are handled by extra mechanisms such as full-page writes or a doublewrite buffer). To prevent that, in a durable configuration both engine types first append a small record to a write-ahead log and fsync it (force it to disk; some engines let you relax this for speed). That append is sequential and fast. Only then does the engine acknowledge the write. After a crash, the log is replayed to rebuild lost changes.
steps.idea: The WAL buys durability cheaply: one sequential append before anything else.
steps.caption: Log record made durable before the ack.

steps.title: LSM: write to memory
steps.body: An LSM tree (log-structured merge tree) takes a different route. After the WAL append, the row goes into the memtable, a sorted structure in RAM such as a skip list (a sorted in-memory structure). No data page is read or modified on disk. Unlike a B-tree update, there is no leaf page to find or read and no page to flush later; the write costs one sequential log append and one in-memory insert, typically about a millisecond or less on a local SSD, depending on the fsync policy.
steps.idea: LSM writes touch only the log and RAM, so they are fast and sequential.
steps.caption: Row lands in the sorted in-memory memtable.

steps.title: Flush to an SSTable
steps.body: When the memtable reaches its limit (RocksDB defaults to 64 MiB), it is frozen and written to disk in one sequential pass as an SSTable: a sorted, immutable file, usually with an index and a Bloom filter (RocksDB needs the filter enabled; it is typically configured). Immutable means never edited again, which makes files simple to cache and copy. The matching WAL segment can now be deleted. New writes go to a fresh memtable.
steps.idea: Flushing turns many random updates into one big sorted sequential file.
steps.caption: Memtable becomes an immutable level-0 SSTable.

steps.title: Reads must look in many places
steps.body: A key may live in the memtable or in any SSTable, and newer data shadows older data. Read amplification means how many files or pages one lookup must check. A lookup checks the memtable, then level-0 (L0) files, the freshly flushed ones, which can overlap, then one file per deeper level. Each SSTable usually has a Bloom filter, a small structure that says 'definitely not here' quickly, so most files are skipped. Without it, a lookup could touch 8 or more files.
steps.idea: LSM reads pay read amplification; Bloom filters keep it to about 1 to 2 disk reads.
steps.caption: Lookup checks newest data first, skipping via Bloom.

steps.title: Compaction cleans up
steps.body: Background compaction merges overlapping SSTables into larger sorted ones at the next level, dropping overwritten values and deleted keys (tombstones). This keeps reads fast and reclaims space, but every byte gets rewritten several times as it moves down the levels. With a size ratio of 10 (each level is 10x bigger than the one above), leveled compaction typically lands around 10 to 30x write amplification, a rule of thumb that varies with workload. Leveled compaction favors reads and space; size-tiered compaction writes less but leaves more files and more duplicate data (space amplification).
steps.idea: Compaction is the bill for fast writes: the same data is rewritten again and again.
steps.caption: Compaction merges files and rewrites them lower down.

steps.title: A write burst outruns compaction
steps.body: Imagine a bulk import pushes writes faster than compaction can merge them. Level-0 files pile up, and each lookup must check more of them, so read latency climbs. To protect itself the engine eventually slows or stalls writers (a write stall) until compaction catches up. Tuning compaction speed and file limits is a core LSM operations task. Bloom filters absorb most of the cost for point lookups, but range scans and cache misses get noticeably slower.
steps.idea: LSM trades smooth latency for throughput; a lagging compaction shows up as slow reads and write stalls.
steps.caption: Backlog: L0 files accumulate, reads get slower.

steps.title: Pick by workload
steps.body: B-trees update pages in place: strong, predictable reads and range scans, pricier random writes. LSM trees buffer writes in memory and merge sorted files later: very high write throughput and compact storage, but read amplification and compaction work. Both use a WAL for crash safety. Write-heavy ingest favors LSM; read-heavy transactional workloads usually favor B-trees. B-tree page rewrites can reach roughly 80-160x for isolated tiny updates, leveled LSM compaction ~10-30x; both are rules of thumb. Postgres and InnoDB use B-trees; RocksDB, Cassandra and HBase use LSM trees.
steps.idea: No free lunch: you choose where to pay, at write time (B-tree) or in the background (LSM).
steps.caption: Two engines, same goal, different cost placement.

quiz.q: A B-tree engine uses 16 KiB pages. An update changes a 100-byte row and the page is written back alone. Roughly how large is the page-level write amplification?
options: About 1x, only the changed bytes are written
quiz.why: 16,384 bytes written for 100 bytes changed is about 160x. In practice several changes to the same page may share one flush, so real numbers are lower.

quiz.q: What does an LSM write avoid that a B-tree update eventually has to do?
options: It never reads or rewrites a data page on the write path; it only appends to the WAL and inserts into the memtable, deferring sorting and merging
It writes directly to the final sorted position on disk
It waits for compaction to finish first
quiz.why: Both engines log to the WAL first. The B-tree must also find, modify and eventually flush a whole page at a random location, which may need a random read first. The LSM defers ordering work to flush and compaction.

quiz.q: An LSM database was fast, then after a huge bulk load its point lookups slow down and L0 file count keeps rising. What is the most likely cause?
options: The memtable is too small to hold any rows
Compaction is falling behind the write rate
quiz.why: Many overlapping L0 files mean each lookup checks more files. That points to compaction not keeping up, and writers may soon be stalled.

quiz.q: The LSM engine holds recent writes in RAM. Why does it still write every change to a WAL?
options: RAM contents vanish on a crash, so the log lets the engine replay unflushed writes
quiz.why: The memtable is volatile. The WAL is a durable, sequential record of writes not yet flushed to an SSTable, replayed after a crash.

quiz.q: A service writes 50k small events per second and rarely reads them back by key. Which engine fits best?
quiz.why: Write-heavy ingest with few reads suits an LSM tree: writes are cheap and sequential, and the read amplification rarely matters.

cheatsheet.def: Sorted tree of fixed-size pages updated in place. Predictable reads and range scans; random, page-sized writes.
Writes go to a memtable, then flush to immutable sorted files merged in the background. Great write throughput.
Write-ahead log: sequential, fsynced record of each change before it is applied, replayed after a crash.
Memtable is the sorted in-RAM buffer; an SSTable is an immutable sorted file on disk, typically with an index and Bloom filter.
Bytes physically written divided by bytes the user wrote. Leveled LSM often runs 10 to 30x; B-trees pay it per page.
Number of places (files or pages) checked per lookup. Low for B-trees; LSM reduces it with Bloom filters and compaction.
Background merge of SSTables that drops overwritten and deleted data (tombstones). Keeps reads fast and limits space amplification (stale data lingering on disk), costs CPU, I/O, and rewrites.
Small probabilistic structure that says a key is definitely not in a file, so lookups skip it. Can give false positives, never false negatives.
